welcome: Day one. Three short lessons: how a vine spends its year, the four rules every licence answers to, and why service alone is not enough.

lessons.intro: Every wine on your list starts as a year in a vineyard. Once you can see that year as a wheel, a lot of wine talk makes sense: why 2021 was a small vintage in parts of France, why a spring frost makes the news, and why a New Zealand wine from the same year is six months 'older' than a French one.

points.p: In winter the vine is dormant and the grower prunes it, choosing how many buds will grow. Bud break follows in spring, when the first green shoots appear. Flowering and fruit set come next: tiny flowers become tiny grapes. Veraison is the moment the grapes soften and change colour, red varieties turning from green to purple. Then ripening, harvest, and the leaves fall as the vine shuts down again.

In Europe bud break is roughly March to April and harvest roughly September to October. In Chile, Argentina, South Africa, Australia and New Zealand the same stages fall about six months later on the calendar, so harvest is around February to April. That is why a Southern Hemisphere wine labelled 2026 was picked months before a Northern one.

The wheel also shows when weather does the most damage. A spring frost just after bud break can kill the new shoots and much of the crop. Cold, wet weather at flowering means poor fruit set, so fewer grapes. Heavy rain near harvest swells and splits berries and invites rot. When a producer says a vintage was 'difficult', it usually means one of these three moments.

lessons.atWork: When a guest asks why a wine costs more this year, or why a favourite is sold out, check whether that region had frost or a wet harvest. 'A spring frost cut the crop' is a better answer than 'prices went up', and it shows the team knows the product.
lessons.takeaway: Read a vintage as a year on the wheel: frost at bud break, rain at flowering, rot at harvest.

lessons.intro: Every alcohol licence in England and Wales is judged against four licensing objectives set by the Licensing Act 2003. The Home Office guidance on the Act, issued under section 182, lists them as the prevention of crime and disorder, public safety, the prevention of public nuisance, and the protection of children from harm. The same guidance says each objective is of equal importance.

points.h: Why they matter on a shift
points.p: The objectives are not paperwork for the owner. They are the test the council and the police apply when a venue applies for a licence, asks to change one, or is called in for a review after complaints. Licensing authorities must have regard to the section 182 guidance and can depart from it only with good reason. Conditions on a licence, such as CCTV, door staff or closing windows, usually trace back to one of the four.

Crime and disorder: refuse service to anyone drunk, keep a refusals log, keep CCTV working. Public safety: never block fire exits, respect the capacity limit, clear broken glass at once. Public nuisance: close doors when music plays and manage smokers late at night, because noise is the most common reason neighbours complain. Children from harm: check age with Challenge 25 and keep a clear policy on under-18s in the bar.

Before you agree to a late party booking, a terrace event or a new drinks promotion, ask four questions. Could it cause trouble? Is anyone at risk? Will the neighbours hear it? Could a child be harmed? If you can answer all four, you are thinking the way a licensing officer does.

lessons.atWork: Pick one objective and check it on your next shift: walk the fire exits, read the refusals log, or listen outside at closing time. Write down one gap and fix it before a licensing officer finds it.
lessons.takeaway: Four objectives, equal weight: crime, safety, nuisance and children. Every licence decision answers to them.

lessons.alt: Two columns at the same table. Service: mains arrive hot and correct, the guest thinks 'fine'. Hospitality: the server hears it is an anniversary and dessert arrives with a signed card, the guest thinks 'they saw us'.
lessons.intro: Will Guidara, who ran Eleven Madison Park in New York when it was named the world's best restaurant, puts it simply in his book Unreasonable Hospitality: service is black and white, hospitality is colour. Service is the technical part: right plate, right seat, on time. Hospitality is how the guest feels about it.

points.p: Service can be trained, timed and checked. Plates land together, from the correct side, at the right temperature. Water is topped up, the bill arrives when asked for. Get this wrong and no warmth will save the evening. But a guest who receives perfect service often leaves thinking only 'that was fine'.

Hospitality starts when a team member engages with the person, not the order. It is hearing that a table is celebrating, seeing that a guest is cold, or remembering how a regular takes their coffee, then acting on it. It is rarely expensive. A signed card, a better table, a word from the manager: what makes it work is that it was meant for them.

Teams often hear 'be more hospitable' as 'smile more'. Make it concrete. In pre-shift, ask each server for one thing they noticed about a guest yesterday and what they did with it. Praise the noticing as much as the action. Over time the team learns that listening is part of the job, not an extra.

lessons.atWork: At your next pre-shift, tell one real story of a moment where the service was correct but the guest felt nothing, and one where a small gesture changed the night. Ask the team which one guests talk about afterwards.
lessons.takeaway: Service gets the plate right. Hospitality makes the guest feel seen. Train both, and praise the noticing.

news.headline: Hospitality Awards UK gala at the Waldorf Hilton on Monday
news.summary: The fourth Hospitality Awards UK takes place on Monday 9 November at The Waldorf Hilton London, Aldwych. It is an invitation-only, black-tie evening recognising achievement across UK hospitality.
news.why: Awards shortlists are a free map of who the industry rates this year. Worth a look for names, venues and managers to learn from.

news.headline: Eating out costs more per visit, but people go out less
news.summary: Lumina Intelligence found average spend per eating-out visit reached £18.35 in the first quarter of 2026, up 5.5% on a year earlier, while the share of people eating out fell to 53.3%.
news.why: Guests are spending more when they come but choosing visits carefully. Every visit has to feel worth it, which is today's hospitality lesson in numbers.

news.headline: Top kitchens drop turbot and lobster as costs soar
news.summary: Starred chefs are cutting expensive dishes. Tommy Banks says turbot rose from £14.50 a kilo in 2018 to £65 a kilo, so his restaurants stopped serving it routinely. St John co-founder Jon Spiteri is also quoted.
news.why: Food cost pressure hits fine dining first. Watch how chefs swap to cheaper fish and cuts without lowering the experience: it is a menu skill you will need.

news.headline: Big Mamma's Edmondo arrives in the City
news.summary: Big Mamma's first site in the City of London, Edmondo, was due to open on 6 November at 6 Lombard Street, near Bank, serving Italian food.
news.why: Its first site in the City, near Bank. When a big group picks a new area, ask why there and why now: footfall, lunch trade and rent decide where a restaurant can work.

news.headline: Tom Booton's first solo restaurant due on Pimlico Road
news.summary: Chef Tom Booton opens his first solo restaurant, modern British, at 87 Pimlico Road on 23 November. Kudu's team also open Braai Bird, rotisserie chicken with South African sauces, in Nunhead on 19 November.
news.why: Two models in one month: a chef's personal restaurant and a tight single-dish concept from an established group. Both are routes to your own place.

try.title: Run a four-objective walk before service
steps: Ten minutes before opening, walk the venue with a notepad.
Check one thing for each objective: CCTV on, fire exits clear, doors and windows ready for music, Challenge 25 sign visible.
At pre-shift, share the one gap you found and who fixes it today.
Then ask each server to bring back one thing they noticed about a guest tonight.
try.why: It turns two of today's lessons into a habit: the licence protected in ten minutes, and the team trained to notice guests.

quiz.q: A frost hits a Burgundy vineyard in mid-April. Which stage of the vine's year is most at risk?
options: Bud break and the new shoots
quiz.why: In the Northern Hemisphere bud break is roughly March to April. A frost then can kill the new shoots and much of the crop.

options: the grapes soften and change colour
quiz.why: Veraison is when berries soften and change colour, red grapes turning from green to purple. Growers use it to estimate harvest.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT one of the four licensing objectives?
options: The protection of children from harm
quiz.why: The four are crime and disorder, public safety, public nuisance and protecting children from harm. Supporting local business is not one of them.

quiz.q: What does the section 182 guidance say about the four objectives?
options: Each objective is of equal importance
quiz.why: Paragraph 1.4 of the guidance says each objective is of equal importance.

quiz.q: A server delivers every course hot, on time and to the right seat, but never talks to the table. In Guidara's terms this is…
quiz.why: That is excellent service: the technical delivery. Hospitality is how the guest feels, and it starts with engaging with them.

terms.def: The point in spring when the vine's buds open and the first green shoots appear. The most frost-sensitive moment of the year.
When grapes soften and change colour, red varieties turning from green to purple. Ripening begins in earnest.
The year the grapes were picked. Southern Hemisphere vintages are harvested about six months before Northern ones of the same year.
The four aims every licence decision must promote under the Licensing Act 2003: crime and disorder, public safety, public nuisance, children from harm.
Home Office guidance on how the Licensing Act 2003 should be applied. Councils must have regard to it.
A hearing where the council reconsiders a venue's licence after a problem is raised. It can add conditions or worse.
How the guest feels about the experience, built by noticing them as people and acting on it.

toolkit.name: Four-objective pre-shift check
items: Crime and disorder: CCTV recording, refusals log to hand
Public safety: every fire exit clear and unlocked, capacity known
Public nuisance: doors and windows plan for music, smokers' area managed
Children from harm: Challenge 25 signs up, under-18s policy briefed

toolkit.name: Service versus hospitality pre-shift prompt
items: What did you notice about a guest yesterday?
What did you do with it?
What could we do tonight for a table like that?
